fetched_contents.text: Rumen methanogens and mitigation of methane emission by anti-methanogenic compounds and substances Abstract Methanogenic archaea reside primarily in the rumen and the lower segments of the intestines of ruminants, where they utilize the reducing equivalents derived from rumen fermentation to reduce carbon dioxide, formic acid, or methylamines to methane (CH4). Research on methanogens in the rumen has attracted great interest in the last decade because CH4 emission from ruminants contributes to global greenhouse gas emission and represents a loss of feed energy. Some DNA-based phylogenetic studies have depicted a diverse and dynamic community of methanogens in the rumen. In the past decade, researchers have focused on elucidating the underpinning that determines and affects the diversity, composition, structure, and dynamics of methanogen community of the rumen. Concurrently, many researchers have attempted to develop and evaluate interventions to mitigate enteric CH4 emission. Although much work has been done using plant secondary metabolites, other approaches such as using nitrate and 3-nitrooxy propanol have also yielded promising results. Most of these antimethanogenic compounds or substances often show inconsistent results among studies and also lead to adverse effects on feed intake and digestion and other aspects of rumen fermentation when fed at doses high enough to achieve effective mitigation. This review provides a brief overview of the rumen methanogens and then an appraisal of most of the antimethanogenic compounds and substances that have been evaluated both in vitro and in vivo. Knowledge gaps and future research needs are also discussed with a focus on methanogens and methane mitigation. Keywords: Anti-methanogenic compound, Methanogen, Mitigation, Protozoa, Rumen Background The unique environment (e.g., relatively rapid passage rate, readily available carbon dioxide (CO2) and hydrogen (H2)) in the rumen helps assemble a community of archaea distinct to that of other anoxic habitats. Nearly all of these archaea are methanogens, most of which are hydrogenotrophic rather than acetoclastic methanogens even though ruminal acetate reaches high concentrations. Rumen methanogens scavenge H2 and CO2 produced by other fermentative members of the ruminal microbiome, producing CH4. Formic acid and methylamines produced by other rumen microbes are also available as substrates for rumen methanogens [1]. Therefore, methanogens interact with other ruminal microbes, including protozoa [2], bacteria [3], and fungi [4], through interspecies H2 transfer. Overall, such interaction benefits the rumen fermentation as it prevents H2 accumulation and feedback inhibition. Most of the methanogens live freely in rumen liquid or as members of the biofilm adhering to feed particles, whereas a small portion of the ruminal methanogens are symbionts, either ectosymbionts or endosymbionts [5]. In co-cultures, a hydrogenotrophic methanogen shifts fermentation towards acetate, increasing ATP yield and growth of cellulolytic bacteria [6]. In vivo studies also showed that inhibition of methanogens decreases acetate: propionate ratio, reflecting a shift of fermentation towards more reduced volatile fatty acids (VFA) than towards acetate [7–9]. Rumen CH4 emission accounts for about 17% of the global CH4 emission [10]. About 2–12% of the ingested feed energy is also lost as CH4 [11]. Therefore, ruminal methanogens have attracted much research interest in the past decade with an aim to understand their diversity and community structure, relationship with other ruminal microbes and with feed efficiency, CH4 emission, and responses to dietary interventions that were intended to mitigate ruminal CH4 emission. Enabled by comprehensive analysis using next generation sequencing (NGS) technologies, new information in the aforementioned aspects has been learned, but contradicting results are also reported, and critical gaps in our knowledge remain. Here we review the current understanding of ruminal methanogens, with an emphasis on protozoa-associated methanogens (PAM) and the responses of ruminal methanogens to anti-CH4 compounds and substances. Future research needs are also discussed. Overview of methanogens present in the rumen The diversity of the rumen methanogens is much smaller, and their diversity is much lower than that of rumen bacteria, with archaeal SSU rRNA only accounting for 6.8% of rumen total SSU rRNA [12]. Archaea in the rumen is represented by <3.3% of the total rRNA (both 16S and 18S) therein. Only eight species of ruminal methanogens have been isolated into pure cultures: Methanobacterium formicicum, Methanobacterium bryantii, Methanobrevibacter ruminantium, Methanobrevibacter millerae, Methanobrevibacter olleyae, Methanomicrobium mobile, Methanoculleus olentangyi, and Methanosarcina barkeri [13]. Recently, five new species were isolated, including Methanobrevibacter boviskoreani (isolated from the rumen of Korean native cattle) [14], Methanobacterium beijingense (isolated from the rumen of goat), Methanoculleus marisnigri (isolated from the rumen of Indian crossbred cattle), Methanoculleus bourgensis (isolated from the rumen of Holstein cattle), and Methanosarcina mazei (isolated from the rumen of Korean Hanwoo cattle) (based on the RDP database). One Thermoplasmatales-like pyrrolysine-dependent archaeon BRNA1 was isolated from bovine (GenBank access number: CP002916). Collectively, 16S rRNA gene sequences from cultured methanogens only accounted for approximately 0.7% of the total archaeal sequences of rumen origin, and several taxa do not have a single cultured representative (Fig. 1). Most of the isolates are members of the family Methanobacteriaceae. Compared to other anaerobic habitats where >100 species of methanogens of 28 genera have been isolated, the diversity and species richness of ruminal methanogens are quite low, reflecting the highly selective ruminal environment for methanogens. fetched_contents.text: The effect and mode of action of saponins on the microbial populations and fermentation in the rumen and ruminant production | Nutrition Research Reviews Introduction The term ‘phytochemicals’ is used to describe non-nutritive plant metabolites that are essential for the survival (i.e. protection against herbivores, pests and micro-organisms) and proper functioning of growth and reproduction in plants(Reference Molyneux, Lee and Gardner1). In recent years, there has been increasing interest among nutritionists and microbiologists to exploit bioactive phytochemicals such as saponins, condensed tannins and essential oils for improving rumen metabolism, and increasing the efficiency of ruminant production(Reference Wallace, McEwan and McIntosh2–Reference Kamra, Patra and Chatterjee7). In particular, bioactive phytochemicals with selective antimicrobial properties can be of interest in animal nutrition(Reference Wallace3, Reference Patra and Saxena8). The impetus behind much of the research of using phytochemicals as feed additives has grown from the necessity of substituting chemical feed additives in animal agriculture because of growing concerns over chemical additives in terms of residues in animal products and the development of bacterial resistance to antibiotics(Reference Barton9). This trend is likely to be continued due to growing demands for organic livestock products. Research is also increasingly being directed at avoiding undesirable impacts of ruminant production on the environment such as contributions to the greenhouse effect, and N and P pollution with the use of safer alternatives to chemical feed additives. Saponins are a group of plant secondary compounds that have shown the possibility to modify rumen fermentation and enhance animal production(Reference Wallace, McEwan and McIntosh2–Reference Wina, Muetzel and Becker5, Reference Patra, Kamra and Agarwal10–Reference Cheeke13). Saponins of Yucca schidigera and Quillaja saponaria have been categorised as ‘generally recognised as safe’ for human consumption by the US Food and Drug Administration(Reference Fenwick, Price, Tsukamoto, D'Mello, Duffus and Duffus14). In recent years, a number of excellent reviews have been published on the potential use of saponins as rumen modifiers(Reference Wallace, McEwan and McIntosh2, Reference Wallace3, Reference Wina, Muetzel and Becker5). However, the mechanisms of action of saponins and discrepancies of results among studies on rumen microbiota and fermentation have not been discussed in details in those reviews. The present review aims to provide deeper insights into the impacts of saponins on the rumen microbial community, how this community can influence rumen metabolism and fermentation, and how this might ultimately lead to improvements in ruminant performance. The recent investigations on the effects of saponins on ruminants are also reported in the present review. Chemistry of saponins The uses of saponins in traditional folk medicines and as a substitute for soap have been known for a long time. They occur in a wide variety of plants and also in some marine animals. Chemically, saponins are a group of high-molecular-weight glycosides in which saccharide chain units (1–8 residues) are linked to a triterpene (triterpene saponins) or steroidal (steroid saponins) aglycone moiety, i.e. sapogenin (Fig. 1). Triterpene saponins are more widely distributed in nature than steroidal types(Reference Hostettmann and Marston15). The steroidal moiety is in most cases in the furostanol or spirostanol form(Reference Hostettmann and Marston15). The saccharide chains are commonly attached at the C3 position (monodesmosidic), but some sapogenins contain two saccharide chains (bidesmosidic) attached at the C3 and C17 (via C28) position(Reference Vincken, Heng and de Groot16). Spirostanol is usually monodesmosidic and furostanol bidesmosidic in nature(Reference Hostettmann and Marston15). Most of the saponins are monodesmosidic or bidesmosidic. However, a lucerne and an Acacia auriculiformis saponin are tridesmosidic(Reference Vincken, Heng and de Groot16). Spirostanol saponins are found mainly in the seeds, roots and bulbs of the plants, whereas furostanol saponins are present in the assimilatory parts of the plants(Reference Hostettmann and Marston15). The number of sugars, the type of sugars (for example, glucose, galactose, xylose, glucuronic acid and rhamnose) and the stereochemistry of the sapogenin moiety with functional groups (–OH, –COOH, –CH3) vary greatly, producing a diverse group of metabolites in this compound class. The chemical structures of triterpene and steroidal saponins are described in detail elsewhere(Reference Hostettmann and Marston15, Reference Vincken, Heng and de Groot16). fetched_contents.text: Meta-analysis on Methane Mitigating Properties of Saponin-rich Sources in the Rumen: Influence of Addition Levels and Plant Sources Abstract Saponins have been considered as promising natural substances for mitigating methane emissions from ruminants. However, studies reported that addition of saponin-rich sources often arrived at contrasting results, i.e. either it decreased methane or it did not. The aim of the present study was to assess ruminal methane emissions through a meta-analytical approach of integrating related studies from published papers which described various levels of different saponin-rich sources being added to ruminant feed. A database was constructed from published literature reporting the addition of saponin-rich sources at various levels and then monitoring ruminal methane emissions in vitro. Accordingly, levels of saponin-rich source additions as well as different saponin sources were specified in the database. Apart from methane, other related rumen fermentation parameters were also included in the database, i.e. organic matter digestibility, gas production, pH, ammonia concentration, short-chain fatty acid profiles and protozoal count. A total of 23 studies comprised of 89 data points met the inclusion criteria. The data obtained were subsequently subjected to a statistical meta-analysis based on mixed model methodology. Accordingly, different studies were treated as random effects whereas levels of saponin-rich source additions or different saponin sources were considered as fixed effects. Model statistics used were p-value and root mean square error. Results showed that an addition of increasing levels of a saponin-rich source decreased methane emission per unit of substrate incubated as well as per unit of total gas produced (p<0.05). There was a decrease in acetate proportion (linear pattern; p<0.001) and an increase in propionate proportion (linear pattern; p<0.001) with increasing levels of saponin. Log protozoal count decreased (p<0.05) at higher saponin levels. Comparing between different saponin-rich sources, all saponin sources, i.e. quillaja, tea and yucca saponins produced less methane per unit of total gas than that of control (p<0.05). Although numerically the order of effectiveness of saponin-rich sources in mitigating methane was yucca>tea>quillaja, statistically they did not differ each other. It can be concluded that methane mitigating properties of saponins in the rumen are level- and source-dependent. Keywords: Saponin, Methane, Rumen, Emission, Fermentation INTRODUCTION The problem of global warming due to accumulation of various green-house gases (GHG) such as carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O) has received serious attention during the past decades. Livestock, especially ruminants, are considered as considerable contributors to the increase in the atmospheric CH4 level, either from enteric fermentation or from manure (Lassey, 2008). A review conducted by Thorpe (2009) showed that annually ruminants produce 80 to 115 Tg CH4. Apart from its contribution to global warming, CH4 emissions from livestock also represents a loss of energy from the animals (Monteny et al., 2006). The amount of energy loss as CH4 within ruminant animals may account for 6% to 10% of gross energy intake, or 8% to 14% of digestible energy intake (Cottle et al., 2011). Such energy loss actually could potentially be conserved, at least partially, for a more useful purpose like production or reproduction. Therefore, effective CH4 mitigation measurements would benefit not only the environment but also the productivity of animals. An approach to mitigate enteric CH4 emission is through nutritional manipulation. Accordingly, various nutritional attempts have been made to mitigate the respective GHG emission, and those could be clustered into ration manipulations, use of additives or biotechnological approaches (Van Nevel and Demeyer, 1996; Takahashi, 2011). Among such nutritional measures, some antibiotics such as monensin, lasalocid and salinomycin had also been tested for their effects in mitigating CH4 with successful applications (Van Nevel and Demeyer, 1996). However, the use of antibiotics as feed additives has received severe criticism due to their potential health risks for consumers. Antibiotics can be accumulated in animal products when being absorbed in digestive tract. They may also pass through the digestive tract (in excreta) and be released into the environment. Through any of these pathways, in turn, the use of antibiotics as feed additives may potentially be harmful to human through development of resistant pathogenic bacteria. A number of countries such as the EU countries have banned such use of antibiotics whilst some other countries are considering banning them (Makkar et al., 2007). Therefore, exploration for natural and safe feed additives that mitigate CH4 emissions while increase productivity of animals simultaneously or at least without hampering the respective productivity is urgently required. Plant secondary compounds such as polyphenols, essential oils and saponins, which are typically high in tropical plants (Kamra et al., 2006; Jayanegara et al., 2011), have been considered as promising natural substances for mitigating CH4 emissions from ruminants. With regard to saponins, some main saponin-rich sources that have been repeatedly tested in relation to CH4 emissions were quillaja, yucca and tea. Indeed, different saponin-rich sources determined the effectiveness of such compounds in mitigating CH4 (Pen et al., 2006) although it still has to be proven across different studies. Apart from source-dependent, levels of saponin additions apparently influenced the response as well. Graded addition levels of saponin-rich sources produced contrasting results, i.e. either decreased CH4 (e.g. Holtshausen et al., 2009) or limited significant effect (e.g. Staerfl et al., 2010). fetched_contents.text: Perspectives on Saponins: Food Functionality and Applications Abstract Saponins are a diverse group of naturally occurring plant secondary metabolites present in a wide range of foods ranging from grains, pulses, and green leaves to sea creatures. They consist of a hydrophilic sugar moiety linked to a lipophilic aglycone, resulting in an amphiphilic nature and unique functional properties. Their amphiphilic structures enable saponins to exhibit surface-active properties, resulting in stable foams and complexes with various molecules. In the context of food applications, saponins are utilized as natural emulsifiers, foaming agents, and stabilizers. They contribute to texture and stability in food products and have potential health benefits, including cholesterol-lowering and anticancer effects. Saponins possess additional bioactivities that make them valuable in the pharmaceutical industry as anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antiviral, and antiparasitic agents to name a few. Saponins can demonstrate cytotoxic activity against cancer cell lines and can also act as adjuvants, enhancing the immune response to vaccines. Their ability to form stable complexes with drugs further expands their potential in drug delivery systems. However, challenges such as bitterness, cytotoxicity, and instability under certain conditions need to be addressed for effective utilization of saponins in foods and related applications. In this paper, we have reviewed the chemistry, functionality, and application aspects of saponins from various plant sources, and have summarized the regulatory aspects of the food-based application of quillaja saponins. Further research to explore the full potential of saponins in improving food quality and human health has been suggested. It is expected that this article will be a useful resource for researchers in food, feed, pharmaceuticals, and material science. Keywords: saponins, emulsifiers, foaming agents, plant extract, food functionality 1. Introduction The name ‘saponin’ is derived from the Latin word ‘sapo’ meaning soap, and associated with the ability to form a soapy foam when plant extract containing saponins is agitated in water [1]. Saponins are a diverse group of compounds widely distributed in the plant kingdom, which are characterized by their structure, which comprises a lipophilic triterpene or steroid aglycone linked to one or more hydrophilic sugar moieties [2,3]. Their structural diversity is reflected in their physicochemical and biological properties. In recent years, consumer demand for natural products coupled with their physicochemical (surfactant) properties and mounting evidence on their biological activity (such as anticancer properties, and hemolytic and hypocholesterolemia activity) has led to the emergence of saponins as commercially important compounds with expanding applications in the food, cosmetics, and pharmaceutical industries [3,4]. Although saponins are known for their health benefits and functional attributes, they also come with some limitations. One of these limitations is associated with their ability to interact with other food components to form complexes, with proteins, lipids, minerals such as iron, zinc, and calcium (insoluble saponin–mineral complexes) negatively influencing the absorption of such food components in the body [5]. Some saponins have limited solubility in water, which can pose challenges in their incorporation and distribution within food matrices. This can affect their effectiveness as emulsifiers or stabilizers in certain food systems [6]. Saponins also find applications in pharmaceuticals and other allied industries [7]. Saponins may help lower blood lipids, reduce cancer risks, and slow blood glucose response [8]. A diet rich in saponins has been suggested to inhibit dental decays and the aggregation of platelets. Saponin consumption has also shown promise in the treatment of hypercalciuria in humans, and as an antidote against acute lead poisoning [8]. Saponins are also used as expectorant and antitussive agents [9]. They are utilized in the cosmetic industry for their ability to act as natural emulsifiers, foaming agents, and cleansing agents. They are constituents of shampoos, soaps, facial cleansers, body washes and shaving creams, contributing to the lathering, cleansing, and moisturizing properties of these products [10]. As the functionality and subsequent applications of saponins are dictated by their composition, a thorough understanding of their chemical and structural features is essential. In addition to their plant origin, such as species and variety, the methods of their extraction and purification play a vital role in saponin composition, structure, functionality, and applications. Saponins are highly researched bioactives, and there are several experimental studies and review articles concerning them. When searching databases such as Google Scholar, PubMed, ScienceDirect, SciFinder, Scopus, and the Web of Science, we found over 32,000 articles that describe the different aspects of saponins. For example, a recent review article [11] highlighted their surfactant properties and applications, whereas Cheok et al. [12] described various techniques for the extraction of saponins. Similarly, El Aziz et al. [13] focused on the chemistry, isolation, and methods of quantification of saponins, and the cytotoxic aspects of saponins are well reviewed elsewhere [14]. A recent review describes the potential of saponins from various sources as antiviral agents [15]. However, there is a scarcity of articles that present a concise overview of the sources, methods of extraction, purification, characterization, quantification, and end-use application of saponins. In addition, regulatory requirements in the food and pharmaceutical application of saponins are also not clearly addressed in previous reviews. node_outputs.N8:
Evidence from experimental studies supporting methane reduction

The experimental evidence for methane reduction by saponins is mixed but generally consistent enough to support the claim that saponins can reduce enteric methane under certain conditions. A meta-analysis of saponin-rich sources found that increasing levels of saponin-rich sources decreased methane emission per unit of substrate incubated and per unit of total gas produced (p < 0.05) [N3-F3]. It also reported a linear decrease in acetate proportion and a linear increase in propionate proportion with higher saponin levels [N3-F3]. These findings suggest a dose-dependent methane-lowering effect, though the meta-analysis also notes that studies reported contrasting results: some showed reduced methane, while others did not [N3-F3]. The meta-analysis further reports that among different saponin sources, quillaja, tea, and yucca saponins all produced less methane per unit of total gas than controls, though the relative effectiveness was not statistically distinguishable across sources [N3-F3].

In vitro evidence is more direct. One study on tea saponin supplementation reported that tea saponin reduced methanogenesis in vitro but increased other effects, with the effect on methane emissions still debated [N3-R2]. Another study on tea saponin in rumen micro-organism cultures found that tea saponin appeared to reduce methane production by inhibiting protozoa and presumably lowering methanogenic activity of protozoal-associated methanogens [N6-R5]. A separate in vitro study on sarsaponin reported that it stimulated mixed ruminal microorganism fermentation while also inhibiting methane production in vitro [N6-R2]. The same meta-analysis also found that saponins decreased rumen ammonia-N concentration in batch cultures [N3-R3]. These results indicate that saponins can alter fermentation end products beyond methane, including reducing ammonia and shifting fermentation toward propionate while decreasing acetate [N3-F3].

The evidence also shows variability across studies and measurement methods. The meta-analysis explicitly states that results varied by addition level and by saponin source, with some studies reporting reduced methane and others not [N3-F3]. In the same meta-analysis, increasing levels of saponin-rich sources reduced methane, but the response was still source-dependent and dose-dependent [N3-F3]. In addition, one review notes that in vivo and in vitro studies on saponins have varied in response, possibly because of differences in study design, diet, and measurement method [N3-R5]. This implies that methane reduction is not universal but depends on the experimental setup.

For total gas, CO2, and other fermentation end products, the evidence is broadly supportive of a fermentation shift rather than merely a methane-specific effect. The meta-analysis found a decrease in acetate proportion and an increase in propionate proportion with higher saponin levels [N3-F3]. It also found a decrease in log protozoal count at higher saponin levels [N3-F3]. A review of saponins on rumen fermentation and production notes that saponins can modify rumen fermentation and enhance animal production [N4-R2], and another review states that saponins are efficient natural rumen modifiers [N4-R3]. These broader fermentation changes suggest that methane reduction is often part of a wider metabolic shift rather than an isolated effect.

Dose-response patterns are a central theme. The meta-analysis found a linear decrease in methane emission with increasing saponin levels [N3-F3]. It also found a linear pattern for acetate proportion decreasing and propionate proportion increasing [N3-F3]. This supports a dose-dependent mechanism, where higher saponin levels generally produce stronger fermentation and methane changes. However, the review of saponin effects on methane and fermentation emphasizes that the response is still debated and varies across studies [N3-R2], which limits the generality of a simple “more saponin, more methane reduction” conclusion.

Overall, the experimental evidence supports methane reduction in some studies and inconsistent responses in others, with the most consistent findings pointing to dose-dependent reductions, protozoa inhibition, and shifts toward propionate and lower acetate [N3-F3][N6-R5][N3-R3]. The evidence is strongest for in vitro and in vivo studies, but the variability across studies and measurement methods remains an important limitation [N3-R5].
node_outputs.N9:
Constraints and practical considerations for using saponins

The main constraints and practical considerations for using saponins in ruminants are toxicity, dose requirements, cost-effectiveness, stability, and feed formulation challenges. The evidence indicates that saponins can be toxic or at least potentially harmful, especially at high doses or when poorly formulated. One review notes that saponins can have adverse effects on ruminants, and several studies on the effect of saponins report both positive and negative roles in animal nutrition [N5-R4]. Another review states that some saponin-containing plants are toxic, and others are undesirable because of toxicity [N5-R4]. A more specific toxicity reference notes that saponins contribute the major toxicity of extracts toward Daphnia magna and Danio rerio, and that saponin degradation products are 3–7 times less toxic than the intact saponins [N5-R2]. While this is not directly about ruminants, it supports the general concern that saponin toxicity can be substantial and may depend on the compound and its degradation state.

Toxicity and adverse effects in ruminants are also implied by the fact that some saponin-containing plants are toxic or undesirable in feeding studies [N5-R3], and that the toxicity of saponins is related to their normal metabolism [N5-R5]. A review on adjuvant effects of saponins notes that Quillaja saponins have been restricted for use in human vaccination because of high toxicity, hemolytic effects, and instability [N5-R1]. While this is human vaccination context, it reinforces the broader concern that saponins can be biologically active to a point of concern. The evidence does not provide a full dose-toxicity profile for ruminants, but it does establish that saponin toxicity is real and can be significant enough to limit practical use.

Dose requirements and cost-effectiveness are another major constraint. The meta-analysis shows that increasing levels of saponin-rich sources reduced methane emission per unit of substrate incubated and per unit of total gas produced, but it also notes that studies arrived at contrasting results, and that the response is level- and source-dependent [N3-F3]. This means that effective methane reduction requires careful dose selection, and that the dose needed may vary by saponin source and by study. The same meta-analysis found that higher saponin levels decreased log protozoal count [N3-F3], but also that the response was not uniform across studies [N3-F3]. A review on saponins in Madhuca longifolia reports toxicity studies and observations of toxic effects using crude total saponins or defatted seed meal [N5-R3], which implies that crude or high-concentration preparations may be more problematic than purified or lower-dose forms. The review also states that some saponin-containing plants are toxic, suggesting that practical use must balance dose against toxicity [N5-R4].

Stability, delivery, and feed formulation challenges are also important. A review on saponins in food functionality notes that some saponins have limited solubility in water, which can pose challenges in incorporation and distribution within food matrices [N4-R1]. This is especially relevant to feed formulation, because poor solubility can reduce bioavailability and effectiveness. Another review describes saponins as amphiphilic compounds with surfactant properties, enabling them to form stable foams and complexes with various molecules [N4-R4]. While this suggests some practical utility in formulation, it also implies that saponins may interact with other feed components in ways that could affect stability or efficacy. The review also mentions that saponins can interact with proteins, lipids, minerals such as iron, zinc, and calcium, forming insoluble saponin–mineral complexes that may negatively influence absorption [N4-F4]. This is a formulation concern because it could reduce nutrient availability and potentially alter overall feed performance.

Taken together, the practical constraints are considerable. Saponins can be toxic, dose requirements vary widely, and higher doses may not be cost-effective or safe [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. Stability and feed formulation are also challenging because some saponins are poorly soluble and may form undesirable complexes [N4-R1][N4-F4]. The evidence therefore supports a cautious practical approach: saponins may be useful, but their use must be carefully dosed, formulated, and monitored for toxicity and feed efficiency [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-F4].
node_outputs.N10:
Variability and inconsistency in methane response to saponins

The methane response to saponins is inconsistent across studies, and the evidence indicates that this inconsistency arises from differences in study design, diet, measurement method, and, to some extent, the saponin source and dose used. The meta-analysis explicitly states that studies reported contrasting results: some showed reduced methane, while others did not [N3-F3]. It also reports that the response was level- and source-dependent, meaning that the same saponin may act differently depending on the dose and the source used [N3-F3]. This variability is a central theme in the evidence and explains why the effect of saponins on methane is still debated in the literature [N3-R2][N3-R5].

Study design differences are a major source of inconsistency. The meta-analysis includes both in vitro and in vivo studies, and the review of saponin effects on methane and fermentation notes that in vivo and in vitro studies have varied in response, possibly because of differences in study design, diet, and measurement method [N3-R5]. This means that the observed methane response can depend on whether the experiment is conducted in a controlled in vitro system or in a living ruminant, on the duration of exposure, and on how methane is measured. The same meta-analysis also notes that the database included multiple studies with different saponin sources and levels, and that the results were treated as random effects while saponin levels and sources were fixed effects [N3-F3]. This statistical structure reinforces that variability is expected across studies and across sources.

Diet and measurement method are additional important variables. The meta-analysis includes studies with different feed types and different saponin-rich sources, and it reports that the methane response was source-dependent [N3-F3]. It also notes that the response varied with addition level [N3-F3]. This suggests that the diet can influence how saponins interact with the rumen microbiota and fermentation products. The review of saponin effects on methane and fermentation similarly states that the effect of saponin supplementation in the ruminant diet on methane emissions is still under debate, highlighting the role of diet in the outcome [N3-R2]. The measurement method is also relevant because the meta-analysis reports that methane was measured using environmental chamber or SF6 methods, and that results varied accordingly [N3-R1]. This means that different measurement techniques can yield different estimates of methane reduction or no reduction.

Variability across feed types and animals is also evident. The meta-analysis reports that different saponin sources produced less methane than control, but the relative effectiveness was not statistically distinguishable across sources [N3-F3]. It also found that higher levels of saponin-rich sources reduced methane, but the response was still source-dependent [N3-F3]. This indicates that the methane response is not consistent across feed types, because different sources and levels can produce different outcomes. The same review notes that the response is still debated and varies across studies [N3-R2], which implies that the effect is not uniform across animals or across feeding contexts.

In summary, the evidence supports a strong conclusion: methane response to saponins is inconsistent, with studies reporting both reduced methane and no effect, and the variation is explained by differences in study design, diet, measurement method, and saponin source and dose [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The response is also likely to depend on the ruminant species, the type of feed, and the specific saponin preparation used [N3-F3][N3-R2]. Therefore, the observed inconsistency is not merely a methodological artifact but a real feature of the biological system being studied.
node_outputs.N7:
Biological pathways by which saponins reduce methane

The biological pathways by which saponins reduce methane are best understood as a combination of direct and indirect effects on rumen microorganisms, with a major role for protozoa, methanogens, and fermentation shifts. The evidence points to saponins interacting with microbial cell membranes and altering fermentation products, while also suggesting that their main effect on methanogens is indirect rather than direct in most studies [N1-F1][N2-F2][N6-R3].

First, saponins interact with rumen microorganisms and cell membranes through their amphiphilic structure. A review describes saponins as amphiphilic compounds that can form stable foams and complexes with various molecules [N4-R4]. Another review explains that saponins are glycosides with a hydrophilic sugar moiety linked to a lipophilic aglycone, giving them an amphiphilic nature and surface-active properties [N4-F4]. This molecular structure is important because it allows saponins to interact with membranes and to disrupt or alter microbial cell surfaces. The review on microbial populations and fermentation also states that saponins inhibit protozoa and that their primary effect appears to be to inhibit protozoa (defaunation), which may increase the efficiency of rumen fermentation [N2-F2]. Integrated explanation of how saponins biologically reduce enteric methane

## 1. Overall conclusion

Saponins can biologically reduce enteric methane emissions, but the evidence is best understood as mixed and context-dependent. The most consistent biological pathway is that saponins act primarily through indirect effects on rumen microorganisms, especially protozoa and protozoa-associated methanogens, while also altering fermentation products and microbial community structure. The same branch reports show that saponins can reduce methane in some studies, increase other fermentation products such as propionate, and reduce acetate and ammonia-N in batch cultures [N3-F3][N3-R3]. At the same time, the response is inconsistent across studies, and practical use faces constraints such as toxicity, dose requirements, and formulation challenges [N3-F3][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-F4]. So the best answer is not “saponins always reduce methane,” but “saponins can reduce methane through microbial and fermentation effects, but the response depends on dose, source, diet, and measurement method.”

## 2. Biological pathways: how saponins interact with rumen microorganisms and cell membranes

Saponins are amphiphilic compounds with a hydrophilic sugar moiety linked to a lipophilic aglycone, giving them surfactant properties and the ability to form stable foams and complexes with various molecules [N4-R4][N4-F4]. This molecular structure is central to their biological action in the rumen. The evidence suggests that saponins interact with microbial cell membranes and microbial surfaces, which is why they are able to inhibit protozoa and alter microbial populations [N4-R4][N4-F4][N2-F2].

A review on the effect and mode of action of saponins states that the primary effect of saponins in the rumen appears to be to inhibit protozoa, which may increase the efficiency of rumen fermentation [N2-F2]. This is a key pathway: saponins do not merely sit in the rumen and wait for methane to form; they actively target protozoa, which are important rumen microbes that can host methanogens and influence hydrogen availability [N2-F2]. Another review notes that saponins may inhibit methane production through defaunating actions and/or directly by decreasing the activities of methanogens [N6-R3]. This shows that the mechanism is not uniform across studies, but the evidence points to a dominant indirect route via protozoa.

## 3. Whether saponins inhibit methanogens directly or indirectly

The branch reports suggest that the effect on methanogens is often indirect rather than direct. A review on rumen methanogens and anti-methanogenic compounds states that saponins probably have little direct effect on methanogens but are known to inhibit rumen protozoa, lowering H2 production and decreasing methane production [N1-R2]. Another review notes that saponins may inhibit methane production through defaunating actions and/or directly by decreasing methanogen activity [N6-R3]. This is important because it shows that some studies support a direct effect, while others emphasize an indirect effect via protozoa.

A related branch report on variability notes that the response is still debated and varies across studies, with some showing reduced methane and others not [N3-R2][N3-R5]. That variability itself supports the idea that the mechanism is not fully uniform. The meta-analysis also reports that higher saponin levels decreased log protozoal count [N3-F3], which reinforces the indirect route through protozoa inhibition. Taken together, the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: saponins can reduce methane mainly by indirectly targeting protozoa and protozoa-associated methanogens, with direct methanogen inhibition reported in some studies but not as the dominant mechanism across the evidence base [N1-R2][N6-R3][N3-F3].

## 4. How fermentation products and microbial community shifts contribute to lower methane

One of the clearest biological effects of saponins is a shift in fermentation products. The meta-analysis found that increasing saponin levels decreased acetate proportion and increased propionate proportion, suggesting a shift toward more reduced volatile fatty acids [N3-F3]. It also found lower rumen ammonia-N concentration in batch cultures [N3-R3]. These changes are important because they alter the fermentation environment in ways that may suppress methanogenesis.

A review on saponins and rumen fermentation states that saponins can modify rumen fermentation and enhance animal production [N4-R2]. Another review describes saponins as efficient natural rumen modifiers [N4-R3]. This means that saponins do not simply reduce methane by an isolated effect on methanogens; they change the broader fermentation profile. The branch report on variability also notes that in vitro and in vivo studies have varied in response, possibly because of differences in study design, diet, and measurement method [N3-R5]. That same variability implies that the fermentation shift is context-dependent and may not always produce the same methane response.

The protozoa-methanogen connection is central here. Protozoa are not merely passive consumers; they can carry methanogens and influence hydrogen availability, which is the fuel for hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis [N1-F1][N6-R5]. When saponins inhibit protozoa, they may lower hydrogen production, reduce protozoa-associated methanogens, and shift fermentation toward propionate [N1-R2][N6-R5][N3-F3]. That explains why methane reduction is often accompanied by changes in fermentation products.

## 5. Evidence from experimental studies

The experimental evidence is mixed but broadly supportive of methane reduction under certain conditions. A meta-analysis found that increasing levels of saponin-rich sources decreased methane emission per unit of substrate incubated and per unit of total gas produced (p < 0.05) [N3-F3]. It also reported a linear decrease in acetate proportion and a linear increase in propionate proportion with higher saponin levels [N3-F3]. These results indicate a dose-dependent effect.

In vitro evidence is also supportive. One study on tea saponin reported that tea saponin reduced methanogenesis in vitro but increased other effects, with the effect on methane emissions still debated [N3-R2]. Another study on tea saponin in rumen micro-organism cultures found that tea saponin appeared to reduce methane production by inhibiting protozoa and presumably lowering methanogenic activity of protozoal-associated methanogens [N6-R5]. A separate in vitro study on sarsaponin reported that it stimulated mixed ruminal microorganism fermentation while also inhibiting methane production in vitro [N6-R2]. These studies show that saponins can reduce methane in controlled in vitro settings.

The evidence also shows variability across studies. The meta-analysis explicitly states that studies reported contrasting results: some showed reduced methane, while others did not [N3-F3]. It also reports that the response was level- and source-dependent, meaning that the same saponin may act differently depending on the dose and the source used [N3-F3]. The review of saponin effects on methane and fermentation notes that in vivo and in vitro studies have varied in response, possibly because of differences in study design, diet, and measurement method [N3-R5]. This means that methane reduction is not universal but depends on the experimental setup.

## 6. Constraints and practical considerations

The practical use of saponins is limited by toxicity, dose requirements, cost-effectiveness, stability, and feed formulation challenges. The evidence indicates that saponins can be toxic or at least potentially harmful, especially at high doses or when poorly formulated. A review notes that saponins can have adverse effects on ruminants, and several studies on the effect of saponins report both positive and negative roles in animal nutrition [N5-R4]. Another review states that some saponin-containing plants are toxic, and others are undesirable because of toxicity [N5-R4]. A more specific toxicity reference notes that saponins contribute the major toxicity of extracts toward Daphnia magna and Danio rerio, and that saponin degradation products are 3–7 times less toxic than the intact saponins [N5-R2]. While this is not directly about ruminants, it supports the general concern that saponin toxicity can be substantial and may depend on the compound and its degradation state.

Dose requirements are also important. The meta-analysis shows that increasing levels of saponin-rich sources reduced methane emission, but it also notes that studies arrived at contrasting results, and that the response is level- and source-dependent [N3-F3]. This means that effective methane reduction requires careful dose selection. A review on saponins in Madhuca longifolia reports toxicity studies and observations of toxic effects using crude total saponins or defatted seed meal [N5-R3], which implies that crude or high-concentration preparations may be more problematic than purified or lower-dose forms.

Stability, delivery, and feed formulation are additional challenges. A review on saponins in food functionality notes that some saponins have limited solubility in water, which can pose challenges in incorporation and distribution within food matrices [N4-R1]. Another review describes saponins as amphiphilic compounds with surfactant properties, enabling them to form stable foams and complexes with various molecules [N4-R4]. While this suggests some practical utility in formulation, it also implies that saponins may interact with other feed components in ways that could affect stability or efficacy. The same review also mentions that saponins can interact with proteins, lipids, minerals such as iron, zinc, and calcium, forming insoluble saponin–mineral complexes that may negatively influence absorption [N4-F4]. This is a formulation concern because it could reduce nutrient availability and potentially alter overall feed performance.

## 7. Why the methane response varies across studies

The methane response to saponins is inconsistent across studies, and the evidence indicates that this inconsistency arises from differences in study design, diet, measurement method, and, to some extent, saponin source and dose. The meta-analysis explicitly states that studies reported contrasting results: some showed reduced methane, while others did not [N3-F3]. It also reports that the response was level- and source-dependent, meaning that the same saponin may act differently depending on the dose and the source used [N3-F3]. This variability is a central theme in the evidence and explains why the effect of saponins on methane is still debated in the literature [N3-R2][N3-R5].

Study design differences are a major source of inconsistency. The meta-analysis includes both in vitro and in vivo studies, and the review of saponin effects on methane and fermentation notes that in vivo and in vitro studies have varied in response, possibly because of differences in study design, diet, and measurement method [N3-R5]. This means that the observed methane response can depend on whether the experiment is conducted in a controlled in vitro system or in a living ruminant, on the duration of exposure, and on how methane is measured. The same meta-analysis also notes that the database included multiple studies with different saponin sources and levels, and that the results were treated as random effects while saponin levels and sources were fixed effects [N3-F3]. This statistical structure reinforces that variability is expected across studies and across sources.

Diet and measurement method are additional important variables. The meta-analysis reports that different saponin sources produced less methane than control, but the relative effectiveness was not statistically distinguishable across sources [N3-F3]. It also notes that the response varied with addition level [N3-F3]. This suggests that the diet can influence how saponins interact with the rumen microbiota and fermentation products. The review of saponin effects on methane and fermentation similarly states that the effect of saponin supplementation in the ruminant diet on methane emissions is still under debate, highlighting the role of diet in the outcome [N3-R2]. The measurement method is also relevant because the meta-analysis reports that methane was measured using environmental chamber or SF6 methods, and that results varied accordingly [N3-R1]. This means that different measurement techniques can yield different estimates of methane reduction or no reduction.

Variability across feed types and animals is also evident. The meta-analysis reports that different saponin sources produced less methane than control, but the relative effectiveness was not statistically distinguishable across sources [N3-F3]. It also found that higher levels of saponin-rich sources reduced methane, but the response was still source-dependent [N3-F3]. This indicates that the methane response is not consistent across feed types, because different sources and levels can produce different outcomes. The same review notes that the response is still debated and varies across studies [N3-R2], which implies that the effect is not uniform across animals or across feeding contexts.

## 8. Bottom line

Saponins biologically reduce enteric methane emissions mainly through indirect effects on rumen microorganisms, especially protozoa and protozoa-associated methanogens. They use their amphiphilic structure to interact with microbial membranes and microbial surfaces, inhibit protozoa, and alter fermentation products such as acetate and propionate [N4-R4][N4-F4][N2-F2][N6-R3][N3-F3]. Some studies also suggest direct effects on methanogens, but the evidence base points more strongly to an indirect mechanism [N1-R2][N6-R3].

At the same time, the response is inconsistent across studies and depends on dose, source, diet, study design, and measurement method [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. Practical use faces real constraints: saponins can be toxic, require careful dosing, and may be difficult to formulate because of limited solubility and interactions with feed components [N5-R4][N5-R2][N5-R3][N4-R1][N4-F4]. So the biological mechanism is clear, but the practical translation into consistent methane reduction is not straightforward.

## 9. Synthesis

If you want a simple one-sentence answer, it would be:  
**Saponins reduce enteric methane mainly by inhibiting rumen protozoa and protozoa-associated methanogens, altering fermentation products such as acetate and propionate, and changing microbial community structure, but the response is inconsistent across studies and depends on dose, source, diet, and measurement method [N1-R2][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-R4][N6-R3].**

The main constraints and practical considerations for using saponins in ruminants are toxicity, dose requirements, cost-effectiveness, stability, and feed formulation challenges. One review notes that saponins can have adverse effects on ruminants, and several studies on the effect of saponins report both positive and negative roles in animal nutrition [N5-R4]. Another review states that some saponin-containing plants are toxic, and others are undesirable because of toxicity [N5-R4]. A more specific toxicity reference notes that saponins contribute the major toxicity of extracts toward Daphnia magna and Danio rerio, and that saponin degradation products are 3–7 times less toxic than the intact saponins [N5-R2]. While this is not directly about ruminants, it supports the general concern that saponin toxicity can be substantial and may depend on the compound and its degradation state.

Toxicity and adverse effects in ruminants are also implied by the fact that some saponin-containing plants are toxic or undesirable in feeding studies [N5-R3], and that the toxicity of saponins is related to their normal metabolism [N5-R5]. A review on adjuvant effects of saponins notes that Quillaja saponins have been restricted for use in human vaccination because of high toxicity, hemolytic effects, and instability [N5-R1]. While this is human vaccination context, it reinforces the broader concern that saponins can be biologically active to a point of concern. The evidence does not provide a full dose-toxicity profile for ruminants, but it does establish that saponin toxicity is real and can be significant enough to limit practical use.

Dose requirements and cost-effectiveness are another major constraint. The meta-analysis shows that increasing levels of saponin-rich sources reduced methane emission per unit of substrate incubated and per unit of total gas produced, but it also notes that studies arrived at contrasting results, and that the response is level- and source-dependent [N3-F3]. This means that effective methane reduction requires careful dose selection, and that the dose needed may vary by saponin source and by study. The same meta-analysis found that higher saponin levels decreased log protozoal count [N3-F3], but also that the response was not uniform across studies [N3-F3]. Another review describes saponins as amphiphilic compounds with surfactant properties, enabling them to form stable foams and complexes with various molecules [N4-R4]. Taken together, the practical constraints are considerable. Saponins can be toxic, dose requirements vary widely, and higher doses may not be cost-effective or safe [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. Integrated explanation of how saponins biologically reduce enteric methane

## 1. Overall conclusion

Saponins can biologically reduce enteric methane emissions, but the evidence is best understood as mixed and context-dependent. The most consistent biological pathway is that saponins act primarily through indirect effects on rumen microorganisms, especially protozoa and protozoa-associated methanogens, while also altering fermentation products and microbial community structure. The same branch reports show that saponins can reduce methane in some studies, increase other fermentation products such as propionate, and reduce acetate and ammonia-N in batch cultures [N3-F3][N3-R3]. At the same time, the response is inconsistent across studies, and practical use faces constraints such as toxicity, dose requirements, and formulation challenges [N3-F3][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-F4]. So the best answer is not “saponins always reduce methane,” but “saponins can reduce methane through microbial and fermentation effects, but the response depends on dose, source, diet, and measurement method.”

## 2. Biological pathways: how saponins interact with rumen microorganisms and cell membranes

Saponins are amphiphilic compounds with a hydrophilic sugar moiety linked to a lipophilic aglycone, giving them surfactant properties and the ability to form stable foams and complexes with various molecules [N4-R4][N4-F4]. This molecular structure is central to their biological action in the rumen. The evidence suggests that saponins interact with microbial cell membranes and microbial surfaces, which is why they are able to inhibit protozoa and alter microbial populations [N4-R4][N4-F4][N2-F2].

A review on the effect and mode of action of saponins states that the primary effect of saponins in the rumen appears to be to inhibit protozoa, which may increase the efficiency of rumen fermentation [N2-F2]. This is a key pathway: saponins do not merely sit in the rumen and wait for methane to form; they actively target protozoa, which are important rumen microbes that can host methanogens and influence hydrogen availability [N2-F2]. Another review notes that saponins may inhibit methane production through defaunating actions and/or directly by decreasing the activities of methanogens [N6-R3]. This shows that the mechanism is not uniform across studies, but the evidence points to a dominant indirect route via protozoa.

## 3. Whether saponins inhibit methanogens directly or indirectly

The branch reports suggest that the effect on methanogens is often indirect rather than direct. A review on rumen methanogens and anti-methanogenic compounds states that saponins probably have little direct effect on methanogens but are known to inhibit rumen protozoa, lowering H2 production and decreasing methane production [N1-R2]. Another review notes that saponins may inhibit methane production through defaunating actions and/or directly by decreasing methanogen activity [N6-R3]. This is important because it shows that some studies support a direct effect, while others emphasize an indirect effect via protozoa.

A related branch report on variability notes that the response is still debated and varies across studies, with some showing reduced methane and others not [N3-R2][N3-R5]. That variability itself supports the idea that the mechanism is not fully uniform. The meta-analysis also reports that higher saponin levels decreased log protozoal count [N3-F3], which reinforces the indirect route through protozoa inhibition. Taken together, the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: saponins can reduce methane mainly by indirectly targeting protozoa and protozoa-associated methanogens, with direct methanogen inhibition reported in some studies but not as the dominant mechanism across the evidence base [N1-R2][N6-R3][N3-F3].

## 4. How fermentation products and microbial community shifts contribute to lower methane

One of the clearest biological effects of saponins is a shift in fermentation products.
